                                    PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                       §              BEFORE THE
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                    §      PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                 §               OF TEXAS

                   ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY’S COMMENTS ON
               THE PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC §25.194

       Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”) files these comments in response to the

Public Utility Commission of Texas’s (the “Commission”) proposal for publication of new 16 Tex.

Admin. Code (“TAC”) §25.194 issued in this rulemaking proceeding on March 12, 2026. Please

refer to Attachment 1 for a redline version of the proposed rule with many of Oncor’s comments

implemented. Oncor appreciates the opportunity to assist with Staff’s efforts to adopt new rules

that implement Senate Bill 6 (“SB 6”).

          I.     ONCOR’S COMMENTS ON THE PROPOSED 16 TAC §25.194

1.     Sections (f)(7) and (f)(9): Oncor recommends that the Commission replace the non-
       refundable interconnection fee and CIAC for direct interconnection costs with a
       take-or-pay rate mechanism.
       Oncor recommends that the Commission replace Section (f)(7), which converts the

$50,000 per MW security interconnecting large load customers provide at the intermediate

agreement stage to a non-refundable interconnection fee at the interconnection agreement stage,

and Section (f)(9), which requires contribution in aid of construction (“CIAC”) for direct

interconnection costs, with a requirement that interconnection agreements include a contractual

commitment in which interconnecting large loads over 200 MW agree to pay rates proportional to

the amount of capacity they contract for, regardless of usage, for at least 10 years after

interconnection.

       Specifically, the Commission should require that the interconnection agreement prescribed

in Section (f) of the proposed rule include terms setting out these capacity-based rates. These

ONCOR’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC
§25.194 – PAGE 1 OF 12
                                                                                               1
 capacity-based charges should follow capacity, not actual demand – even if an interconnected large

load fails to interconnect or meet its load ramp or reduces demand significantly, it would still be

obligated to pay the full amount of its capacity charges until the capacity is made available for

reallocation. In this way, the take-or-pay mechanism would mitigate concerns regarding delayed

load ramps or customers who fail to interconnect because the customer is required to pay for the

capacity it reserved regardless. Though, an allowance should be made for the electric utility’s

ability to serve the large load; the rule should require the interconnecting large load to pay a

minimum demand charge based on the lesser of its maximum requested peak demand and the

capacity made available by the interconnecting utility at the time. The rule should require that the

$50,000 per MW security provided as part of the intermediate agreement be converted to an

amount necessary to secure capacity-based rate payments for the lesser of three years and the

remaining payment term. A payment term of at least 10 years after the interconnecting large load

interconnects will appropriately promote financial commitment.

       Implementing capacity-based rates would provide a range of benefits: (1) they would

incentivize loads to be more precise in their load requests in order to minimize payment for excess

capacity; (2) as rates are paid for this contracted-for capacity, they would mitigate rate increases

for other ERCOT ratepayers; (3) such a system would allow loads to pay for and hold capacity

during a ramp-up period; and (4) these rates would closely align with principles of cost causation

as transmission and distribution utilities must plan for and build to loads’ contracted capacities.

Finally, these capacity-based rates fit well within Senate Bill 6’s requirement that the Commission

consider new rates that better assign transmission costs.

       Further, the nonrefundable $50,000 per MW fee in proposed rule Section (f)(7) should not

be included in the Commission’s rule and should be replaced by capacity-based rates because



ONCOR’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC
§25.194 – PAGE 2 OF 12
                                                                                                   2
 Senate Bill 6 does not contemplate the conversion of the per MW security provided by a large load

customer under PURA § 37.0561(h)(1) to a nonrefundable fee. And PURA § 37.0561(i)

specifically requires per MW security be refunded after it’s applied to any outstanding amounts

owed. The proposed fee likely contravenes Senate Bill 6’s intent.

       CIAC for direct interconnection costs under proposed rule Section (f)(9) should also be

replaced by capacity-based rates because CIAC does not appropriately socialize the costs of

standard interconnection facilities across ERCOT customers or allow utilities to earn a fair rate of

return on their facilities. Electric utilities are legally entitled to earn a return on the value of the

assets employed for public convenience. CIAC is a direct offset to an electric utility’s rate base,

meaning that electric utilities earn no return on these facilities even though they construct, manage,

and continually maintain them. Greatly increasing the portion of electric utility facilities covered

by CIAC would greatly increase the value of assets managed by electric utilities that are not

included in their rate bases, driving down utility financial standing at a time when they are being

asked to raise unprecedented levels of capital to invest in the Texas grid.         Oncor’s proposed

capacity-based rate mechanism substantially mitigates these utility ratemaking concerns and is a

more effective solution than CIAC for direct interconnection costs because it ensures that

interconnecting large loads with high direct interconnection costs cover these costs through rates.

2.     Section (f): Oncor recommends that the Commission extend the deadline to execute
       an interconnection agreement to 60 days.
       Section (f) of the proposed rule requires that a large load customer must execute an

interconnection agreement with the interconnecting DSP or TSP within 30 days of completion of

the interconnection study. Oncor recommends that the Commission lengthen this window to 60

days, a time period that gives the parties a reasonable amount of time to negotiate and draft an

interconnection agreement.       Not only does a 30-day window leave insufficient time for

ONCOR’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC
§25.194 – PAGE 3 OF 12
                                                                                                       3
 interconnection agreement negotiations, it does not leave the interconnecting utility enough time

to accurately estimate the amount of security required for significant equipment or services under

Section (f)(8) of the proposed rule and the amount of CIAC required to cover direct interconnection

costs under Section (f)(9) of the proposed rule. Further, after utilities ascertain the required

security amounts, a 30-day window would likely leave customers with insufficient time to gather

and post security.

       A 30-day window could only be practicable if the Commission prescribed a standard large

load interconnection agreement. Oncor recommends that the Commission implement a standard

large load interconnection agreement similar in function to the existing standard generation

interconnection agreement. Oncor recommends that this standard large load interconnection

agreement cover both the intermediate agreement requirements of Section (d) and the

interconnection agreement requirements of Section (f) by starting as an intermediate agreement

and converting to a full interconnection agreement at the appropriate point. This would both

streamline the negotiation and execution of interconnection agreements and solve problems

created by differing interconnection agreements. Non-standardized interconnection agreements

have created uncertainty in the ERCOT process, as different utility agreements are treated

disparately. A standardized agreement will also promote equal access to the Texas grid by

eliminating the patchwork of current interconnection agreement terms.

3.     Sections (g)-(h): Oncor recommends that the Commission modify the rule to
       contemplate a full refund of any security remaining after it’s applied to any
       outstanding amounts owed to the interconnecting utility.
       Oncor recommends that the Commission modify Section (g) of the proposed rule to allow

interconnecting customers that withdraw all or a portion of requested peak demand or contracted

peak demand to receive a refund of the balance of their security after applying it to any outstanding



ONCOR’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC
§25.194 – PAGE 4 OF 12
                                                                                                    4
 amount owed. Similarly, Oncor recommends that the Commission modify Section (f) to allow the

same refund for any non-utilized capacity. Customers under Sections (g) and (f) are already subject

to pancaking financial commitments: nonrefundable CIAC for interconnection costs, all other

costs incurred by the interconnecting DSP or TSP, nonrefundable $50,000 per MW interconnection

fee at the interconnection agreement stage, and the risks and costs associated with posting $50,000

per MW security, security for significant equipment or service, and security for system upgrades.

There is no need to add to those commitments by arbitrarily confiscating 80% of a customer’s

posted security associated with withdrawn or missed capacity, especially if the Commission

accepts Oncor’s recommended take-or-pay mechanism proposed in Section 1 of these comments,

above.

4.       Oncor recommends that the Commission allow security obligations to overlap to
         prevent a pancaking of financial security obligations.
         Oncor recommends that the Commission allow the required financial commitments in the

interconnection agreement phase to overlap, not stack. As discussed in Section 3, above, an

interconnecting customer at the interconnection agreement stage is required to pay CIAC for

interconnection costs, pay all other costs incurred by the interconnecting DSP or TSP, pay a

nonrefundable $50,000 per MW interconnection fee, and post security for significant equipment

or service and security for system upgrades under the proposed rule. These commitments cover

far more than the direct costs caused by the interconnecting customer and even the greater system

impact. For that, CIAC for direct interconnection costs (or the capacity-based method Oncor

proposes, above) and security for system upgrades alone are sufficient. It is unclear what costs the

$50,000 per MW nonrefundable fee and the security for significant equipment or services cover

beyond what is already covered by CIAC and security for system upgrades required under the

interconnection agreement.      If the Commission keeps this full package of overlapping

ONCOR’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC
§25.194 – PAGE 5 OF 12
                                                                                                   5
 interconnection agreement financial commitment requirements in its final rule, it runs the risk of

stifling the interconnection of new large loads and discouraging business development in direct

opposition to the express purposes of Senate Bill 6 under PURA § 37.0561(b).

5.     Sections (d)(2) and (f)(2): Oncor recommends that the Commission strengthen the
       “substantially similar interconnection request” disclosure rules to include projects
       pursued by contracted end users.
       Oncor recommends that the Commission strengthen the “substantially similar

interconnection request” disclosure language in both Section (d)(2), at the intermediate agreement

stage, and Section (f)(2), at the interconnection agreement stage. Currently, the language only

requires the entity requesting interconnection to disclose its own substantially similar requests.

This allows end users to sidestep this requirement by using various developers as proxies. These

developers can each submit one of multiple substantially similar requests and would not need to

disclose the other substantially similar requests submitted by other developers for the same end

user. The rule should be modified to look through the requesting entity to the end user.

6.     Section (f)(10): Oncor recommends the Commission require ERCOT to allocate
       responsibility for system upgrades and clarify how the “system upgrades that are
       necessary to reliably serve the large load customer” will be securitized.
       Oncor recommends that ERCOT be required to allocate the amounts of security required

from each interconnecting large load to securitize “system upgrades that are necessary to reliably

serve the large load customer” under Section (f)(10) of the proposed rule through the batch study

process. Also, Oncor recommends that the Commission clarify how the security amounts under

(f)(10) will be calculated. Deciding which system upgrades “are necessary to reliably serve the

large load customer” in advance of requiring the customer to post security to cover a portion of

those system upgrades at the interconnection agreement stage introduces significant modeling

challenges that could delay the batch study and interconnection process. Many commenters,



ONCOR’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC
§25.194 – PAGE 6 OF 12
                                                                                                 6
 including Oncor, provided extensive feedback to the Commission in prior comments regarding the

modeling challenges associated with apportioning system upgrade responsibility to

interconnecting large loads in the CIAC context. Since then, the Commission removed CIAC for

system upgrades and added security for system upgrades. This new security language raises the

same modeling concerns.

       The rule would require ERCOT, through the batch study process, or the interconnecting

utility to determine which future system upgrades are “necessary” for each interconnecting large

load, then the interconnecting utility would need to estimate the specific cost of these upgrades,

both before executing the interconnection agreement and beginning construction on the system

upgrades and interconnecting the customer.        The RTOs that have attempted to allocate

responsibility for transmission network upgrades in the generation context (e.g., Southwest Power

Pool and Midcontinent Independent System Operator) have been plagued with multi-year

interconnection delays for new projects.

       Oncor is not aware of any method for allocating responsibility for system upgrades among

multiple large load customers based on usage or any other variable. The extent to which a given

customer “uses” a transmission asset cannot be conclusively modeled. Grid modeling examines

the effects of multiple contingencies and scenarios on how power could flow across the system.

The directions and magnitudes of power flows across the system vary widely depending on the

modeled contingency or scenario. One contingency or scenario may result in a given large load

“using” nearly all the capacity of a system upgrade, while another may result in the load using

none of the upgrade’s capacity at all. And these determinations are bound to prove contentious

and may result in contested cases that delay the interconnection of many subsequent large loads

for years.



ONCOR’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC
§25.194 – PAGE 7 OF 12
                                                                                                 7
         Further, reallocating the securitization of “necessary” system upgrades when new large

loads interconnect adds another layer of unneeded complexity and delay. Presuming that security

would be required from subsequent interconnecting customers for already-securitized “necessary”

system upgrades, ERCOT or interconnecting utilities would need to refund a certain portion of

security to the batch of initial interconnecting large loads and shift responsibility onto newly

interconnecting loads.

         The complexities of determining the responsibility of interconnecting large loads for

“necessary” system upgrades and reallocating responsibility as new large load customers

interconnect only multiply with the future introduction of an ERCOT batch study process. There

is no reasonable way to discern which large load customer included in a batch is the cause of, and

therefore should be responsible for securitizing, a system upgrade when the studied large loads are

modeled together in a single batch. And if multiple large load customers in a batch are deemed

causes of a system upgrade, the same allocation challenges described above will grind the

construction of these new required system upgrades to a halt.

7.      Oncor recommends that the proposed rule not specifically split responsibility
        between DSPs and TSPs or do so in a standard large load agreement.
        Oncor recommends that the Commission modify the rule to not dictate the specific split of

responsibilities between DSPs and TSPs, but instead simply require that utilities in these multi-

utility scenarios execute an agreement that allocates relevant critical interconnection

responsibilities as the parties see fit.

        The Commission should appropriately accommodate the diversity of utility practices by

not requiring a set allocation or the inclusion of an allocation in a specific agreement. The

Commission should allow utilities to allocate responsibilities in either the intermediate or

interconnection agreements, or in a separate agreement entirely. The agreement should include


ONCOR’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC
§25.194 – PAGE 8 OF 12
                                                                                                  8
 the large load customer, the retail utility, and any transmission service providers and should at least

allocate responsibility for collection of financial security and CIAC, collection of required

customer disclosures, submission of large load forecasting data to ERCOT, management of any

initial study, management of the Large Load Interconnection Study (“LLIS”), and submission of

LLIS results to ERCOT.

       Alternatively, if the Commission decides to adopt a standard large load interconnection

agreement that covers both the intermediate agreement requirements in Section (d) of the proposed

rule and the interconnection agreement requirements in Section (f), Oncor recommends that the

Commission designate the roles and responsibilities of DSPs and TSPs to the extent necessary in

the standard agreement. Also, if the Commission decides to explicitly divide responsibilities

within the rule or within a standard agreement, it should ensure that this division is compatible

with the roles spelled out in PGRR 145.

8.     Section (e): Oncor recommends that the Commission modify the rule to leave room
       for the coming ERCOT batch study process.
       Additionally, Oncor recommends that the Commission modify the latest discussion draft

to leave room for a future shift to an ERCOT-led initial batch study process. As ERCOT shifts

towards a centralized batch study process, it is likely that the batch study process that

simultaneously includes prospective large loads across the system would yield the most accurate

and detailed initial study. The rule should require the interconnecting utility to either complete a

utility-driven initial study or submit information necessary for inclusion of the large load customer

in an initial study to ERCOT within 30 days of executing the large load interconnection screening

agreement, whichever is applicable.

9.     Section (e): Oncor recommends that the Commission require an interconnecting
       large load to both execute and fund an intermediate agreement prior to ERCOT or
       the interconnecting utility beginning its study.

ONCOR’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC
§25.194 – PAGE 9 OF 12
                                                                                                      9
        Oncor recommends that the Commission modify Section (e) of the proposed rule to require

that an interconnecting large load both execute and fund an intermediate agreement, including

providing all financial commitments under the agreement, before the interconnecting utility begins

its study of proposed large load interconnection or ERCOT includes it in a study batch.

10.    Section (e)(4): Oncor recommends that the Commission modify its rule to require an
       interconnecting large load that materially changes its load ramp schedule during the
       study process to submit a new interconnection request to the interconnecting utility.
       Oncor recommends that the Commission modify its rule to require an interconnecting large

load that materially changes its load ramp schedule during the study process to submit a new

interconnection request to the interconnecting utility. A material modification of a load ramp

schedule warrants a fresh interconnection study because it could significantly change the

feasibility of the interconnection and the interconnection facilities and upgrades required. Oncor

recommends that the Commission adopt the materiality qualifier requiring a new interconnection

request if an interconnecting large load experiences (1) a 6-month change in load ramp or (2) a 75-

MW change in peak load.

                                    II.   CONCLUSION

       Oncor appreciates the opportunity to assist with Staff’s evaluations pursuant to Senate Bill

6.

 1   The Public Utility Commission of Texas (commission) proposes new 16 Texas Administrative

 2   Code (TAC) §25.194 relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards. This proposed rule will

 3   implement Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) §37.0561, as enacted by Senate Bill (SB) 6

 4   during the Texas 89th Regular Legislative Session. The new rule will implement new PURA

 5   §37.0561, which requires the commission to establish standards for interconnecting large load

 6   customers in the ERCOT power region in a manner designed to support business development in

 8   reliability. The new rule will require a large load customer, before the large load customer can be

 9   included in an ERCOT interconnection study, to execute an intermediate agreement that requires

12   30 days after ERCOT completes the interconnection study, to execute an interconnection

13   agreement that requires the large load customer to update its disclosures, pay a non-refundable

14   interconnection fee in the amount of $50,000 per MW; post financial security for significant

15   equipment or services; pay contribution in aid of construction for direct interconnection costs; and

16   post financial security for system upgrades.      Additionally, the new rule will set forth the

 1   §25.194. Large Load Interconnection Standards.

 2   (a)    Purpose and Scope. This section sets forth the standards and criteria for an electric utility,

 3          a municipally owned utility, and electric cooperative to interconnect a large load customer

 4          to the ERCOT system. Nothing in this section limits the authority of a municipally owned

 5          utility or an electric cooperative to impose electric service requirements for large load

          I.       ONCOR'S COMMENTS ON THE PROPOSED 16 TAC §25.194

1.     Sections (f)(7) and (f)(9): Oncor recommends that the Commission replace the non-
       refundable interconnection fee and CIAC for direct interconnection costs with a
       take-or-pay rate mechanism.
       Oncor recommends that the Commission replace Section (f)(7), which converts the

$50,000 per MW security interconnecting large load customers provide at the intermediate

agreement stage to a non-refundable interconnection fee at the interconnection agreement stage,

and Section (f)(9), which requires contribution in aid of construction ("CIAC") for direct

interconnection costs, with a requirement that interconnection agreements include a contractual

commitment in which interconnecting large loads over 200 MW agree to pay rates proportional to

the amount of capacity they contract for, regardless of usage, for at least 10 years after

interconnection.

       Specifically, the Commission should require that the interconnection agreement prescribed

in Section (f) of the proposed rule include terms setting out these capacity-based rates. These

 capacity-based charges should follow capacity, not actual demand - even if an interconnected large

load fails to interconnect or meet its load ramp or reduces demand significantly, it would still be

obligated to pay the full amount of its capacity charges until the capacity is made available for

reallocation. In this way, the take-or-pay mechanism would mitigate concerns regarding delayed

load ramps or customers who fail to interconnect because the customer is required to pay for the

capacity it reserved regardless. Though, an allowance should be made for the electric utility's

ability to serve the large load; the rule should require the interconnecting large load to pay a

minimum demand charge based on the lesser of its maximum requested peak demand and the

capacity made available by the interconnecting utility at the time. The rule should require that the

$50,000 per MW security provided as part of the intermediate agreement be converted to an

amount necessary to secure capacity-based rate payments for the lesser of three years and the

remaining payment term. A payment term of at least 10 years after the interconnecting large load

interconnects will appropriately promote financial commitment.

       Implementing capacity-based rates would provide a range of benefits: (1) they would

incentivize loads to be more precise in their load requests in order to minimize payment for excess

capacity; (2) as rates are paid for this contracted-for capacity, they would mitigate rate increases

for other ERCOT ratepayers; (3) such a system would allow loads to pay for and hold capacity

during a ramp-up period; and (4) these rates would closely align with principles of cost causation

as transmission and distribution utilities must plan for and build to loads' contracted capacities.

Finally, these capacity-based rates fit well within Senate Bill 6's requirement that the Commission

consider new rates that better assign transmission costs.

be included in the Commission's rule and should be replaced by capacity-based rates because

 Senate Bill 6 does not contemplate the conversion ofthe per MW security provided by a large load

        CIAC for direct interconnection costs under proposed rule Section (f)(9) should also be

replaced by capacity-based rates because CIAC does not appropriately socialize the costs of

standard interconnection facilities across ERCOT customers or allow utilities to earn a fair rate of

return on their facilities. Electric utilities are legally entitled to earn a return on the value of the

assets employed for public convenience. CIAC is a direct offset to an electric utility's rate base,

meaning that electric utilities earn no return on these facilities even though they construct, manage,

and continually maintain them. Greatly increasing the portion of electric utility facilities covered

by CIAC would greatly increase the value of assets managed by electric utilities that are not

included in their rate bases, driving down utility financial standing at a time when they are being

asked to raise unprecedented levels of capital to invest in the Texas grid.         Oncor's proposed

capacity-based rate mechanism substantially mitigates these utility ratemaking concerns and is a

more effective solution than CIAC for direct interconnection costs because it ensures that

interconnecting large loads with high direct interconnection costs cover these costs through rates.

 1   The Public Utility Commission of Texas (commission) proposes new 16 Texas Administrative

 2   Code (TAC) §25.194 relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards. This proposed rule will

 3   implement Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) §37.0561, as enacted by Senate Bill (SB) 6

 4   during the Texas 89th Regular Legislative Session. The new rule will implement new PURA

 5   §37.0561, which requires the commission to establish standards for interconnecting large load

 6   customers in the ERCOT power region in a manner designed to support business development in

 7   this state while minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system

 8   reliability. The new rule will require a large load customer, before the large load customer can be

 9   included in an ERCOT interconnection study, to execute an intermediate agreement that requires

10   the large load customer to provide certain disclosures and post financial security in the amount of

11   $50,000 per megawatt (MW). The new rule will also require a large load customer, not later than

12   30 days after ERCOT completes the interconnection study, to execute an interconnection

13   agreement that requires the large load customer to update its disclosures, pay a non-refundable

14   interconnection fee in the amount of $50,000 per MW; post financial security for significant

15   equipment or services; pay contribution in aid of construction for direct interconnection costs; and

16   post financial security for system upgrades.      Additionally, the new rule will set forth the

 1   §25.194. Large Load Interconnection Standards.

 2   (a)    Purpose and Scope. This section sets forth the standards and criteria for an electric utility,

 3          a municipally owned utility, and electric cooperative to interconnect a large load customer

 4          to the ERCOT system. Nothing in this section limits the authority of a municipally owned

 5          utility or an electric cooperative to impose electric service requirements for large load

 6          customers on their systems in addition to the standards adopted under this section.

 8   (b)    Applicability. This section applies to a large load customer that seeks:

10          (2)    an expanded interconnection that equals or exceeds 75 MW for the first time; and

11          (3)    an expanded interconnection that exceeds 75 MW by 75 MW or more.
